utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic Sainovic and Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I have an indication, first of all, of the parties appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Tom Hannis. I represent the Prosecution. On my left is Ms. Christina Moeller, who will address issues regarding the expert the witnesses this afternoon. And on my right is Ms. Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. For Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Eugene O'Sullivan and Slobodan Zecevic appearing for Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. For Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Tomislav Visnjic, on behalf of General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. And for Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Vladimir Petrovic on behalf of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Now, gentlemen, because there was no 65 ter Conference, it may take a little longer than normal to deal with this today, and I may seem a little more at sea even than I normally am. So I'm looking to you for possibly a little more assistance than would otherwise be the case. And I'll try to deal with or raise at least the issues that I'm aware of in some sort of logical order. My most recent involvement in this case was the hearing for the recovery of documents from the various NATO member states. All I can do today is indicate the state of play in that motion. The Chamber have already deliberated on the matter, and a decision is in the course of preparation. What I can't say is how long any further deliberations will take or when exactly the decision will be issued, but I anticipate perhaps in about two weeks or so from now there will be a decision on that matter. I don't think you can anticipate it much before that certainly. The second issue I would like to raise is the attempts that have been made and are ongoing to try to reach agreement on certain facts. I can see that there has been correspondence exchanged on that, and that has gone on for some time. It has not so far been very productive, and what I'd like to do is see whether any assistance can be offered in either directing minds on the issue or, alternatively, deciding just how much more effort ought to be put into it. Now, either the Prosecution or, I think, Mr. Petrovic, either of you is -- is best placed, I think, as being most recently involved in dealing with this. So which of you would like to try to bring me up to date on that one? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I'll try to provide you with information on the situation and I will try to provide a lengthy explanation of the strategy followed by Defence counsel in this matter. From the very beginning of discussion on agreed facts, our position has been to try and go beyond the contents of the indictment or the pre-trial brief itself. The indictment and the pre-trial brief contain a fairly minor number of facts. These facts are not very extensive and don't have to do with the substance of our defence of Mr. Sainovic. As a result, our approach has been that apart from focussing on the contents of the indictment itself, we should also propose certain facts that will certainly be examined at the appropriate time. So we would not only like to deal with what is stated in the indictment. We would also like to raise issues that we believe are of importance for the defence of Mr. Sainovic, especially once we commence with the trial stage. For this purpose, we have already forwarded about three letters referring to about 15 facts to the Prosecution. The first group of facts was not accepted. The second group of facts was agreed to entirely, and that's what is stated in the Prosecution pre-trial brief. Just before the Christmas recess, we also provided a list of a third group of 18 facts, and a few days ago we received a preliminary response from the Prosecution to that letter that we forwarded to them. Our position is that the preliminary response opens up the possibility of engaging in further discussions on those facts. Some of the facts have been agreed on, or in certain cases there's room to agree on certain facts; whereas, there are certain facts that the Prosecution will not agree on. But we believe that this is the right procedure that we should follow. And the conclusion of this procedure -- the outcome of this procedure should be that we will manage to agree on a large number of facts. The Prosecution has suggested a certain position that has been accepted by the Defence. The second letter that we forwarded had to do with what was stated in the indictment itself. We believe that this is important, but that we should go beyond the scope of the indictment or the facts mentioned in the indictment. We will respond to the last letter that we received from the Prosecution on the 14th of January. We will provide a detailed response to that letter. And I believe that we will be able to make headway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. Now, Mr. Hannis, there doesn't seem to me on the face of it to be anything wrong in principle with the Defence seeking and trying to reach agreement with the Prosecution on matters which are outwith the strict end of the indictment if it can be shown that these are relevant to the Defence case. I note from the letter that you sent to Mr. Petrovic that you take quite a firm line that seeking such agreement is really beyond what ought to be done here. Nevertheless, Mr. Petrovic seems to think that the door is ajar. Now, what is the Prosecution position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it -- once the proposed facts from the Defence go outside the boundaries of the indictment, it is harder for us to find ourselves in the position of being able to agree to those facts for a couple of reasons: One is once it gets outside the scope of our document, frankly I'm new to this case and I'm not familiar with all the background, so if it's just a proposal of an agreed fact without some supporting document or a reference to a witness statement or a transcript somewhere, it's really hard for me to know whether that's something I can agree to. Also, it's hard for me to know because I'm not fully familiar with the defence in the pre-trial brief as to what aspect of the defence it might agree to. It's also partly a matter of timing. Some of those facts it seems to me might be more appropriate later in the case or might be unnecessary later in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it though that you accept that it may be appropriate to agree facts even though they are out with the terms of the document if they are relevant to the Defence case. You accept that principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do. I'm not categorically opposed to that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, on that basis, it does seem to me there's room for progress to be made at least in further discussions and I don't think I need to address the matter any further, at least so far as Mr. Sainovic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And I hope our letter made it clear to the Defence and to the Court that we were remaining recall open to the possibility of further discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there a point to be made on behalf of either of the other accused in relation to attempt to agree facts? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. The -- so far as working with the Prosecution, as part of our response to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, which was filed last September, we included in that response to the Prosecution pre-trial brief the facts based solely on the indictment to which we were prepared to stipulate. So we have not attempted or discussed with the Prosecution anything outside the bounds of the indictment itself and we've notified them of the facts we agree with in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, no -- nothing concerns you in this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have also completed the phase that had to do with agreed facts. But I would like to point out that just before this Status Conference, we received a certain amount of material from the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 68, and it might be appropriate to re-launch this process because it's obvious that some of the information we were provided with is beneficial to the accused and it might form the basis for new discussions with the Prosecution in relation to some other facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I simply note that there may be further discussion with -- with you, Mr. Visnjic. Now, the next matter that may require clarification is the state of play in relation to the witnesses whom the Prosecution propose to present via Rule 92 bis. Now, is there any assistance that the Court can provide at this stage? I see Mr. O'Sullivan has, I think, taken the lead to some extent on this subject. Do you, Mr. O'Sullivan, consider that there's any assistance I can provide at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think so, Your Honour. We've met with Mr. Hannis and Ms. Moeller just prior to this conference, and I think we're at the stage where we can attempt to establish contact with the group of 11, which are of particular importance and have immediate importance to the -- this 92 bis process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your note to Mr. Boas, you raise the question of meeting witnesses without a representative of the Prosecution being present, and you go on to say: "We note furthermore that two of the 11 witnesses are employees of NGOs or a government agency. One of them is an unidentified Rule 70 witness, and we can see no reason why these individuals should meet with the Defence." Do you mean should not meet with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Should not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So you're satisfied that your own efforts are sufficient at the moment to ensure that there's a -- satisfactory arrangements made for you to take such information as you require from the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think. But as between the -- the Prosecution and the Defence, we're on the right track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it also, Mr. Hannis there's nothing more I need do at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. That takes me then to the subject of expert reports. Can I say, first of all, that -- that there is an issue over the question whether the Trial Chamber can decide at this stage that an expert's report should not be admissible. And we have submissions from the parties on that. That preliminary question, in other words, whether it's appropriate at all for the Trial Chamber to meddle, especially when it's a Chamber that may not be dealing with the trial, is one that will be addressed by the Chamber in due course. And I -- I don't think I need to look further at that. But there are issues over, I think, four expert reports which are not fully disclosed as yet. And I have to say that in regard to each of them, I have fairly major concerns and, therefore, I'm look for reassurance about how these should be dealt with. So, Mr. Hannis, I think I look to you on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Moeller is ready to deal with those expert witnesses

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you made that clear. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I start with the latest developments concerning one of the expert reports, the expert report for the DNA expert, Mr. Alonso, where they completed disclosure as of today with disclosing the English translation of the fourth component of his report. So we could say that this report is now -- sorry, the B/C/S version. The English version has already been disclosed a week ago. The B/C/S version of the report. So the Defence is now in possession of the complete report in English and B/C/S version. So there is no reason to be concerned about this report any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So should I now be making an order about the responses of the Defence to the report of Mr. Alonso?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. According to Rule 94 bis, unless you order otherwise, the Defence would now have 30 days to file their notice to you regarding whether they want to cross-examine the expert, or whether they accept the report as it stands. And we would assume that this clock would be starting to tick now, unless you order otherwise, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Going on to the constitutional expert, you are aware of the history, I think, from the Prosecution report we filed on the 28th of October, 2004. And it has taken us quite a long time to actually find a constitutional expert for the reasons we set out in the report, actually going even back into the Milosevic case, where we had a similar situation. We informed you that in October last year we identified three potential experts and we contacted one of them and entered into discussions with him. Then we contacted the other two to try to find out which would be the most suitable. And we managed to actually make our determination and to meet with this expert last Thursday and Friday on the 13th and 14th. He was here in The Hague and we managed to discuss all the details pertaining to his report and the conditions of his expert testimony. And he agreed to accept our commission on that and to provide the report. Now he informed us as to the disclosure deadline that he would not be able to start preparing this report before February and that he would need two months. So we are confident that we could disclose the final report in early April or end of March. He's very much aware of the urgency of this matter and promised us to do his utmost to speed it up, but he's a very busy man, also teaching at the university, and has other competing obligations in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're paying attention to the current evidence in the Milosevic trial, which -- which will have a direct bearing, I imagine, on -- on the work of your constitutional expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And it was a very happy coincidence that he was here actually last week when the evidence was already led in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things that's emerging from that evidence is there's a great deal of factual material about decisions taken and alterations made to the rules of the constitution about which one, I imagine, could stipulate what the exact impact of these might be. Maybe then the question for exploration with the expert. But it seems to me that -- that a great deal of time can actually be spent in court on material about which there probably isn't any real issue between the parties in either that case or this one. But, of course, if you have the advantage of counsel in a case such as this one, then you may be able to save a great deal of time by stipulating about the factual background on which hopefully by the time your constitutional expert has completed his work there really isn't much dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a very good suggestion that we can take further with the Defence. Specifically pertaining to these issues which haven't been addressed explicitly now, but we are certainly ready to -- to enter into discussions on this point. And I think the -- the report will really boil down to the interpretation of these factual issues, and we will very much try to limit it to these factors and not to -- to overburden it with unnecessary factual considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, what -- what the constitution of the Republic of Serbia was and -- and how it was changed in relation to Kosovo are matters which it now appears are clearly documented but -- but which in the course of the Milosevic trial has been very difficult to identify the -- the best documentation on over quite a considerable period. So that's -- there is useful current -- there are useful current developments there for this case. Now, there are two more to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you deal with -- well, which one to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: However you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with the military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The military expert report, also you find our basic submissions and our report filed on 28th October, 2004. And the problems we described therein is that we have a number -- a high number of outstanding documents that still need to be either translated or even locked and summarily translated for the analyst to determine whether they are of value or not to his report, and need to be considered or not. According to the situation we described in the report, there are 375 documents that we received in February 2004. Now the status quo relating to these documents is that they all have been locked and that summary translations have been provided in the meantime so that the military expert was able on the basis of the summary translations to decide which of these almost 400 documents are really relevant. These are 59 documents, and they are still now awaiting the complete translation. And then they, of course, need to be analysed by him and considered for the report. Then there is another installment of documents we received only later this year, which are 78 documents, and we are -- for these documents we are at the stage they have been locked. They have been submitted to the Evidence Unit. But we have not yet managed -- or the expert has not yet managed to decide on the basis of summary translations which of these documents are really needed for his report. So this is one step earlier than regarding the other documents which were received in spring last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This does seem to be too open-ended, I think. All three accused have been in detention now for a considerable period of time. The expert we're dealing with here has provided reports in relation to the matters which are the subject of this trial, also previously. But at the moment, as I understand it in this case, there is no report at all. There is some sort of general summary of -- of certain material but no -- no actual report. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, that's not the situation. For the military expert, we have actually a report already. But it's not the final report. It's not the updated version containing all these new documents. But there is a report which contains more than 200 pages, I think, which has been disclosed to the Defence on 18, 19, and 31st January 2003. So they're in possession of these 200 pages of original report and the underlying material as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, what then about the sexual assault expert?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The sexual assault expert in the situation is the following: For her the situation is a bit different from the constitutional expert, for instance, because she is not an academic person; she's a field worker. And the situation that she has never testified as an expert witness before has created some more complications than actually discussing and designing her report than it has with other experts. That's why we weren't in a position to disclose the final version at the time we filed our pre-trial submissions in June 2004 but only an outline of her report. Due to her also competing other professional obligations for Medicum Mondialo [phoen], where she works in the field offices with victims in Kosovo and elsewhere, she could only meet us again here at The Hague in December last year to finalise our discussions on -- on the amendments to her report. In particular, what we were missing in her report were additional facts and some data from -- from the work of Medica Mondiale, which we think is crucial for the Trial Chamber to have. We discussed with her the possibility of obtaining these additional aspects, and she agreed that she could do so within two months as she had to go back to colleagues in the field office providing this data in particular. This is why we request that -- to be allowed to disclose this report in early March. And I'm -- we are in contact with -- with the expert, and she has reconfirmed with me just recently that she will be able to provide the report in late February or early March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the nature of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The nature of this evidence, it's relating to the sexual assault charges that are contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- in the indictment, and it gives a general background on the problems faced in dealing with these specific crimes in the context of the Kosovarian culture and society. Because I think -- we think -- the Prosecution thinks that this is a very important aspect for the Trial Chamber to consider when evaluating the evidence we can present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Moeller. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I would have comments on the military expert, Your Honour, which as you know is the subject of a pending motion and response from the Defence. The problem we have with -- with the request by the Prosecution is that they requested that you allow them to file the military expert report only after a trial date is set in this matter, and we see no reason for any delay whatsoever once the expert has had an opportunity to work with the translations, and it appears that that process is moving along quickly. And we think the expert should file his report as soon as practicable and not have any time frame for disclosure based on a trial date. As for the sexual assault --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go on to that, just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, just to be clear about this, you say that there's a motion from the Prosecution to be allowed not to disclose this report until after the trial date has been set or after the trial has commenced?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe the motion requests that the -- Philip Coo's report be disclosed once the trial date is set, and we've responded to that by saying that there's no basis for any such delay and that when he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe it was October last year. And our response followed within the two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a filing, I think, submitted on the 28th of October. Is that the document -- that document contains a motion, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the one, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at page nine, paragraph 17, and it says: "The Prosecution submits it would be in the interests of justice if he were allowed to submit the final version of his military expert report at a time closer to the tile trial date once it is set," meaning once the trial date is set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, on the other expert, anything else to be said?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just on the sexual assault expert, I have to confess that it's a little unclear to me exactly what this -- the purpose of the report is or what the tenor of this report is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The timing now looks not out of the way in view of the fact that there's no date set for the trial as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And just so it doesn't slip by, Your Honour, that we do have a response to that October filing of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said that -- you say it's before the Trial Chamber. Is there any reason why I can't deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's none, no. You can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, anything to be said on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wish to add that we have been informed by Ms. Featherstone that there is a possibility that a trial date might be set within about eight weeks after we receive notice that it's been set. I only wish to say that should this really happen, we will certainly not be in a position to be prepared unless Philip Coo's report is disclosed before that date or before that notice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief. I have two points I wish to make: First, the Defence of Mr. Sainovic feels that what Mr. O'Sullivan has said is reasonable and noteworthy. We feel that the Trial Chamber should set a precise deadline for the disclosure of the military expert report and all other expert reports. Secondly, I wish to say that with all due respect and understanding for the heavy obligations on our learned friends, it seems to me that the competing professional duties of their experts should not cause undue delay for our clients, in view of the fact that Mr. Sainovic has been in detention for almost three years. Someone's professional obligations are not sufficient reason to prevent more efficient disclosure. With all due respect and all understanding for the difficulties of our learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Petrovic, your point -- your last point is well made. I think it's resolved -- well, the issues are resolved in relation to the other experts by the passage of time alone. But there is an issue outstanding in relation to Mr. Coo. Ms. Moeller, does this -- the Prosecution have control over the prioritising of translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, very little, if any. The situation in general with regard to translations is that all proceedings which are not in trial have no priority. So we are generally -- all our requests are not handled as priority requests as long as we are in pre-trial stage. And with regard to particular translations, it is very difficult to track actually with the Translation Unit and to receive some response as to when translations can be expected. We tried to do that with regard to the documents I just referred to regarding Phil Coo, the 59 documents, and we got a rather weak answer that it may be March this year. But we are more or less in the hands of the Translation Unit in this regard. And maybe to give you the full picture of the situation, it's also worth mentioning that in last summer there was a period of about eight weeks when there was a full stop in translation of even accepting new requests. We couldn't even hand in new requests for new translations for a period of almost two months because they were so overburdened. And we can only with very good reasons require to be put on an urgent -- on -- to -- sorry, to request to have special urgency for -- for a particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there -- there may be one avenue that we could explore. One would think that the Philip Coo report is also important to the Milosevic proceedings. And that case is in trial. And so if there's a way to move these documents up the list, it may be in the related trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have to bear in mind that that trial is already in the Defence phase and what we're talking about here is a report by a Prosecution expert who gave evidence some time ago. What I shall do in relation to that matter is have the Trial Chamber consider it in the context in which you initially indicated it had been presented in October. So far as the others are concerned, I envisage that the next Status Conference will be around the 14th of April. So I shall order a disclosure of the report by the constitutional expert by the 7th of April. And I shall order disclosure of the report of the sexual offence expert by the 20th of March. And I simply note that as far as Mr. Alonso is concerned, the clock is already ticking and that no one's made a motion to any other effect. Now, the next item I have noted is an application by the Prosecution for modification of the reporting regime with an associated motion on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic for disclosure. Perhaps I ought to hear in this instance, first of all, from Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday the Prosecution filed a response to our motion. I received the response today, as I was away yesterday. We will probably be filing our reply to this response in the near future, and I believe that we will then present our final arguments in that reply. So at this point in time, I have nothing to add to what is already stated in the motion, and I received the response shortly before this Status Conference, so I really haven't had the time to examine the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to that matter, I guess we'll await their reply. As far as the reporting regime, we just suggested that change because we thought it was a more efficient use of resources. The witness is in a position where matters don't change much from month to month and it seems a waste of time for the Court to have to read nothing new, nothing new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One even more efficient use of resources might be for you to delete the witness from the list, since you haven't found him or her. And this is a witness you can't trace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We -- we -- I hesitate to speak more fully for -- for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I think we -- we know where this witness is. It's a matter of how we go about contacting him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the motion from Mr. Ojdanic suggests some doubt about whether there are any other witnesses whose identity has not been disclosed to the Defence. I mean, is there uncertainly about what the issues are on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are some -- on our witness list, I think the very last number, 144, refers to some Rule 70 witnesses for whom we do not have approval from the Rule 70 providers about the -- the terms and conditions under which those witnesses will be allowed to testify according to them, and we have to make applications according to what those providers require of us. We've been told by one of the providers that they won't address our application with regard to their witness until we have a trial date in this case because their position on what they will allow and what they would require will depend on the point in time where we are when the witnesses would be anticipated to appear. But it would be our intention, Your Honour, in that event -- it would not be a matter of us notifying the Court and the Defence, that now we know who this Rule 70 witness is and we'd like to put him on tomorrow. We won't -- we won't do that. We won't interfere with the Defence's right to have adequate time to prepare to deal with those witnesses when they know who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, one point that's made by the Prosecution is that you have stated on record that you will not start investigation and preparation of the Defence case in the absence of additional funding before the trial stage of the case is entered. Now, has that changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I have the request before me, it was at the Status Conference on the 12th of May, 2004. In the meantime, the situation has changed in that we have been granted additional funds. And even in such a situation, even if we did not have sufficient funds, I believe that it is our right to select items and give priority to certain items when preparing for the case and it is nevertheless the Prosecution's obligation to disclose material in good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking questions about this is this is one of these issues that do crop up quite a lot in this Tribunal, I've discovered very quickly, which on the face of them should not require the intervention of a Trial Chamber or a Judge -- a Pre-Trial Judge. It should be possible for sufficient exchange to take place between Prosecution and Defence, for responsible counsel to take responsible decisions about how much an issue must be pressed, a reasonable position of the Prosecution is, in seeking to delay disclosure. I make these remarks in the hope that this issue might be resolved. But if it's not, then I think it's simply one that I will have to deal with. I don't think this is for the Trial Chamber. It's one I will deal with on the basis of the written filings, once you've responded, as you indicate, Mr. Visnjic. But could I suggest that before you respond, it might be worth having a word with the Prosecution to see if in fact there is a real issue here that -- if the -- if the evidence is important enough or the -- the lack of time might turn out to be significant enough for this to be an issue that requires the intervention -- or my intervention. For the moment, I simply note the position. Now, the last point I've noted is that each of the accused has again applied for provisional release. I -- all I can do, I think on that, is indicate how it will be treated. A history of -- of the applications which have already been made and the determinations that have been made will be prepared. And against that background, I will consider each of these applications. I suspect I will then remit them to the Trial Chamber for further consideration. That will be dealt with fairly soon, in view of the significance of the issues that are raised by such applications. But in view of the history, it may take a little time for the -- certainly for me to become completely familiar with the background and for the Chamber to deal with these. But hopefully, again, within the course of the next two weeks or so it will be possible to address these issues. Now, that completes the agenda that I had noted for this conference. Is there any matter any counsel wishes to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I in the e-mail responses for additional matters by the Prosecution, I had referred to one document we had received relating to the accused Mr. Sainovic. It actually pertains more to the issue of provisional release because it pertains to some proceedings ongoing in the Belgrade district court in which there apparently is a request for his presence at this time. And I perhaps should have better filed it as a -- as a supplement -- a supplementary pleading. But because we were here and we were all going to be together, I had just mentioned that. And I'm happy to follow the Court's direction as to whether I should simply submit that document as a annex or a supplement to the pleadings filed in connection with his motion for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two other things, Your Honour, regarding the expert reports. I think you set the date for the sexual assault expert to file her report by the 20th of March, which I believe is a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh. Do you want the 18th or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 21st, if possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And related to the expert reports, Your Honour, I think those deadlines are fine, based on our discussions with the expert. I think they'll have no problem getting the reports completed by that date. I have less confidence in whether or not we'll be able to have a translation in the language of the accused by those dates because of the bottleneck we discussed before, but we will make our best efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis. I'd overlooked the point you make about the attendance of Mr. Sainovic at Belgrade. Are you saying that the Prosecution will be seeking to have him transferred to attend there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I only indicated that that request had been sent to the Registrar and to our office as well. And with regard to the issue of provisional release and what conditions he might be released upon, it seemed to be a factor that needed to be considered by the Court. Because I don't know what would be required of him in connection with that if he were provisionally released here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it mentioned in your response on the question of provision until release?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not because we didn't have it at hand at the time we filed that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you ought to make a filing in relation to this so that it's not lost sight of in considering the questions of provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'd just very briefly like to address an issue. The crimes that -- what my colleague has been speaking about are mentioned in the second and third request for provisional release. Unfortunately, my colleagues omitted to provide a response to that. I believe this is an opportunity for them to respond in an appropriate way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, gentlemen. The next Status Conference, I indicated earlier, could be the 14th of April, unless anyone has a particular reason for avoiding that date. Very well. I fix the next Status Conference for Thursday, the 14th of April at 3.00 p.m. Meanwhile, the court is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: at 4.11 p.m.
